item.title: Identifying level-$k$ reasoning in repeated games: Strategies, beliefs, and cognitive ability
item.description: arXiv:2610.33098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we identify level-$k$ reasoning in repeated games that operates at the level of a supergame strategy. First, we develop a model of level-$k$ reasoning that incorporates choices over strategies as well as beliefs about the strategies chosen by others. Then, jointly using elicited strategies and beliefs about strategies from the indefinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, and applying a new notion of balance-optimal error tolerance, we classify a substantial fraction of subjects as level-1 or level-2. Moreover, we show that when level-$k$ reasoning operates at the level of a repeated-game strategy, cognitive ability and experience predict higher level reasoning.
item.dc:creator: David Gill, Yaroslav Rosokha

item.title: A Stationary Mean-Field Model for Carbon Market Stability Reserve
item.description: arXiv:2610.33132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate the design of a market stability reserve as a stationary mean-field singular control problem. The allowance balance follows a regime-switching diffusion, while the regulator injects or withdraws allowances through bounded-variation controls. The objective trades off the average allowance balance, its stationary dispersion, deviations from a long-run target, and intervention costs. The optimal policy is a regime-dependent band rule characterized by four reflecting thresholds. Its computation reduces to a scalar fixed-point problem combining a coupled variational inequality with the invariant distribution of the reflected process. A calibration to the EU ETS yields thresholds of the same order of magnitude as the existing Market Stability Reserve rule. Comparative statics show that volatility is the main determinant of the intervention band, whereas the frequency and duration of crisis regimes have limited effects. A simpler two-threshold policy based on average regime dynamics closely reproduces the optimal regime-dependent policy in terms of liquidity and intervention volumes.
item.dc:creator: Ren\'e A\"id, Federico Cannerozzi, Giorgio Ferrari

item.title: Observable Self-Restraint in Repeated Cheap Talk
item.description: arXiv:2610.33390v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A long-lived sender repeatedly advises a myopic receiver who observes only the recommendation record. Nonbinding, observable self-restraint, such as a rolling quota on favorable recommendations, makes each favorable recommendation use capacity that could serve future opportunities, inducing selective advice. With two actions, when obedience requires a strictly positive cost of self-restraint, the sender's normalized equilibrium payoff is subject to a ceiling equal to the payoff from the best credible partitional signal minus the expected cost of self-restraint. This bound holds at every discount factor; under an upper-tail condition, rolling quotas approach it as the sender becomes patient. A sufficiently valuable opportunity can also induce an informative violation that ends communication.
item.dc:creator: Haohui Wang

item.title: Conference Design for Consensus under KL Acceptance
item.description: arXiv:2610.33555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study consensus formation and information acquisition in conferences where DeGroot-type opinion updating is constrained by an acceptance rule based on Kullback-Leibler divergence. Players choose private information experiments before deliberation, and these choices determine both their posterior distributions and acceptance tolerances. We establish sufficient conditions for global consensus under specified conference structures, including repeated bilateral conferences organized by a fully receptive mediator. Under full reimbursement of the mediator's conference costs, the information-acquisition game has a weighted potential and admits a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. We develop a numerical procedure using verified payoff bounds over the continuous posterior domain to certify approximate equilibria and assess partial reimbursement policies that preserve a given equilibrium profile. The binary state, three-player examples illustrate how conference order interacts with state variance. At larger variances in the tested range, placing the demanding nonmediator last is associated with lower conference costs and lower certified sufficient planner reimbursement, but greater information acquisition expenditure by the mediator. These findings reveal a trade-off between the planner's fiscal expenditure and the mediator's private burden, and show that the conference structure matters economically.
item.dc:creator: Liping Tang, Michiko Ogaku

item.title: Stable matching under regulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.34412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a market in which any coalition can reach agreements, a stable outcome need not exist even when agents have substitutable preferences. We show how regulation can restore stability. If a regulator participates in every agreement, a setwise stable outcome exists when each ordinary agent's preference satisfies a condition weaker than substitutability, while the regulator's preference remains largely unrestricted. An alternative existence result allows ordinary agents to have arbitrary preferences while requiring the regulator to support each agent's profitable contract deletions. Our results apply to matching markets involving regulated activities.
item.dc:creator: Chao Huang

item.title: The fiscal limits of efficient trade
item.description: arXiv:2610.34460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sustaining efficient trade under private information requires external subsidies. Although a designer cannot avoid deficits on average, they can control exposure. We characterize efficient and truthful mechanisms that minimize the worst-case deficit in markets with many buyers and sellers, under interim participation. This problem is dual to maximizing expected trade surplus under correlation ambiguity, with constraints on submarkets with one agent removed. In bilateral trade, the best deficit ceiling is the competitive surplus in a benchmark continuum market, achieved by a "competitive pivot mechanism". In larger markets, optimal mechanisms are characterized in terms of worst-case residual welfare contributions, but solutions exhibit a complex combinatorial structure. We obtain explicit guarantees under natural participation charge restrictions and establish how the best deficit excess decays as market thickens. Our duality characterization is general and extends to many mechanism design environments (public goods, partnership dissolution), and alternative participation constraints.
item.dc:creator: Toan Le, Saara H\"am\"al\"ainen, C\'esar Barilla

item.title: Screening AI-equipped applicants
item.description: arXiv:2610.34508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI can lower the cost of producing polished application materials without improving applicants' abilities to do the job. We study an employer who observes qualifications and work history, summarized by observable quality, but must infer other job-relevant attributes from reports that applicants can manipulate at costs that depend on privately known manipulation ability. The employer commits to a hiring rule under a capacity constraint, and we evaluate rules by match value net of applicants' manipulation costs. We show that, as manipulation ability becomes increasingly dispersed among applicants with the same observable quality, socially optimal hiring converges to selection on observable quality alone, a phenomenon we call strategic feature collapse. To capture the remaining welfare gain from reports, we construct a simple dual-track mechanism that directly admits applicants with high observable quality and offers some otherwise excluded applicants a report-based route to admission. Despite the complexity of multidimensional screening, this mechanism is asymptotically optimal under additional regularity, matching the unrestricted optimum's welfare gain from reports through second order.
item.dc:creator: Pengyu Qian, Sophie H. Yu

item.title: Equilibrium Existence in Oligopoly Pricing and Consumer Search
item.description: arXiv:2610.34578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper revisits the consumer search and price competition model of Wolinsky (1986). Suppose that the market has a finite number of firms, and the match value distribution function and survival function are both log-concave. Then, there is a unique symmetric pure-strategy equilibrium price with active consumer search. Two applications are discussed.
item.dc:creator: Yue Li

item.title: Revealed Convex Preference
item.description: arXiv:2610.34771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Convexity of preferences is a pervasive assumption in economic analysis, so it is important to understand how this property is revealed in data. In this paper, we develop a method to test for convexity given partial preference information in the form of weak and strict incomplete orders. We characterize the pairs that can be extended to convex preferences and provide an efficient algorithm to verify this property. Requiring the convex preference to align with an order that satisfies independence, such as the Euclidean order or stochastic dominance, does not complicate the test. We apply our results to consumer demand, choice under risk and uncertainty, and preferences over information, and establish conditions under which upper semicontinuity or continuity can also be obtained. We identify environments in which convexity imposes no additional restrictions beyond rationality, extending Afriat-type results to infinite data and co-convex budgets and establishing a convex version of exact rationalization.
item.dc:creator: John K. -H. Quah, Rui Tang

item.title: Extremal Perfect Monotone Equilibria in Bayesian Games with Strategic Complementarities
item.description: arXiv:2610.35511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study sharp bounds on equilibrium behavior in Bayesian games when players may make mistakes. Under strategic complementarities, the set of behavioral perfect equilibria has a largest and a smallest element, both in pure strategies. We ask when these bounds are monotone and how they depend on the way mistakes are made. For monotone supermodular games, we consider limits of equilibria under increasing perturbations, in the sense that conditional tremble distributions have full support and increase stochastically with type. We show that the largest and smallest perfect equilibria exist, which are pure and monotone. Under the general perfection notion, the extremal perfect equilibria continue to be monotone in the setting with finite actions. With infinite actions, the extremal perfect equilibria can be nonmonotone, and the set of perfect monotone equilibria can even lack extrema.
item.dc:creator: Wei He, Yeneng Sun, Hanping Xu

item.title: Self-Confirming Equilibrium under Model Misspecification
item.description: arXiv:2610.35692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the steady states of games played recurrently within large anonymous populations of players who receive partial ex-post feedback about the play of their opponents. Departing from the classical Bayesian account, players do not trust their conjectures as a correct description of the strategic environment but consider them as approximations of a reality that is only partially modeled and partially observed. We introduce games with feedback and uncertainty attitudes, in which the normal-form structure is enriched with a profile of feedback functions and, for each player, a preference functional that encodes aversion to misspecification and to ambiguity. The induced misspecification sensitive criterion contains the variational, maxmin, and smooth-ambiguity evaluations as special cases and collapses to expected utility when beliefs are unambiguous and the player is neutral to misspecification. The appropriate steady-state notion for such games is the Self-Confirming Equilibrium under Model Misspecification (SCEM), which requires each player to best respond to a set of structured conjectures that the feedback generated by equilibrium play cannot falsify. In contrast with the classical theory and with its ambiguity-averse extensions, mixed-strategy Nash Equilibria need not be self-confirming. We therefore develop a companion notion of Robust Nash Equilibrium (R-NE), in which every supported action remains optimal under a variational evaluation. Robust Nash equilibria refine SCEM, exist whenever the statistical distances are continuous, thereby delivering existence of SCEM, and coincide with the latter under fully informative feedback. Under observationally consistent divergences and observable payoffs, R-NE and SCEM reduce, respectively, to Nash equilibrium and Self-Confirming Equilibrium under Ambiguity (SCEA), which generalizes smooth self-confirming equilibrium.
item.dc:creator: Riccardo Formenti

item.title: Joint Service Depth and Priority Design in Queueing Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.33334v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In AI-assisted service systems, the server can choose how much processing effort to spend on each job, which we call the service depth. Deeper reasoning improves output quality but occupies the server longer and increases congestion, and the realized processing time remains random because AI models are probabilistic and tasks vary in complexity. We study the joint design of service depth and priority in a single-server queue whose customers differ in delay sensitivity, with the goal of maximizing social welfare. For each customer type, the decision maker chooses a priority level and a service depth, and service times are exponential with mean equal to the chosen depth. With two customer types and linear service values, we characterize the centralized optimum. Counterintuitively, it prioritizes the patient type and gives it a smaller service depth when patient customers are sufficiently prevalent. When delay sensitivity is private, however, incentive compatibility requires the impatient type to receive a weakly shorter sojourn time, so the optimal price menu never prioritizes the patient type. Consequently, there can be a welfare gap between the centralized decision maker's optimal control policy and the optimal decentralized pricing mechanism. With a continuum of types, the centralized optimum is monotone: more delay-sensitive customers receive weakly smaller depth and higher priority, so the optimum can be implemented by a price menu with no welfare loss. Allowing randomized depths similarly closes the gap in the two-type model. Finally, we calibrate an agentic AI service system using published coding-agent trials from DeepSWE and numerically examine priority inversion, the value of joint design, and the welfare gain from personalization.
item.dc:creator: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Yash Kanoria, Jonathan Y. Tan

item.title: A Comparison of Cursed Sequential Equilibrium and Sequential Cursed Equilibrium: Different Concepts of Cursedness in Dynamic Games
item.description: arXiv:2304.05515v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cursed Equilibrium of Eyster and Rabin (2005) has been a leading theory for explaining winner's-curse-type behavior in static Bayesian games, but it faces conceptual limitations when applied to dynamic games. Two recent extensions, Cursed Sequential Equilibrium (CSE) by Fong, Lin and Palfrey (2025) and Sequential Cursed Equilibrium (SCE) by Cohen and Li (2026), address these limitations in fundamentally different ways. Complementing these two papers, this paper provides a systematic comparison of CSE and SCE, clarifying their conceptual foundations and technical implications, including their notions of cursedness, belief updating, treatment of public histories, and relationship to cursed equilibrium in one-stage Bayesian games.
item.dc:creator: Meng-Jhang Fong, Po-Hsuan Lin, Thomas R. Palfrey

item.title: Breaking Ties among Equals: Serial and Sequential Dictatorships in House Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2407.14101v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the deterministic allocation of indivisible objects to agents under unit demand and strict preferences, without monetary transfers. When every agent must receive an object, two agents who report identical preferences cannot be treated equally, so every mechanism embodies a rule for breaking such ties. We introduce two invariance requirements on this rule. Fair treatment of equals requires the favored member of every preference-identical pair to be the same at all profiles; the weaker pairwise tie-breaking allows the favored member to depend on the reports of the other agents but not on the pair's common report. Combined with non-wastefulness and strategy-proofness, (i) fair treatment of equals characterizes the serial dictatorships, (ii) pairwise tie-breaking and non-bossiness characterize the sequential dictatorships, and (iii) pairwise tie-breaking and the identical-preference lower bound---which compares each agent's assignment with her outcome when everyone shares her ranking---characterize the serial dictatorships once again. When agents may remain unassigned, the first two characterizations extend upon adding individual rationality, but the identical-preference lower bound no longer forces a fixed order. Among sequential dictatorships, the identical-preference lower bound is equivalent to boundedness: there is a priority whose $k$th-ranked agent is called after at most $k-1$ real objects have been assigned.
item.dc:creator: Di Feng, Jacob Coreno

item.title: The pursuit of happiness
item.description: arXiv:2506.10537v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies populations of individuals -- that we call homo-felix -- who maximise an objective function that we call happiness. The happiness of one individual depends on the payoffs that they receive in games they play with their peers as well as on the happiness of the peers they interact with, and on their status. Individuals care more or less about others depending on whether that makes them more or less happy. This paper analyses the ``happiness feedback loops'' that result from these interactions in simple settings. We find that individuals revise their other-regarding attitudes in terms of relative comparisons. In particular, individuals tend to care more about individuals who are happier than them, while spiteful behavior may emerge only under poor socio-economic conditions and is directed towards the worst off individuals. Such general results are illustrated by studying simple 2 x 2 games, where we find that homo-felix can converge to a variety of equilibria which includes but goes beyond Nash equilibria, and in an $n$-persons public good game.
item.dc:creator: Debora Princepe, Onofrio Mazzarisi, Erol Akcay, Simon A. Levin, Matteo Marsili

item.title: Representation in District-Based Elections
item.description: arXiv:2602.12910v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: District-based elections must reconcile two objectives: representing each district's electorate and matching the statewide delegation to parties' vote shares. We study seat allocation rules when these objectives conflict. The optimal rules, characterized by a cutoff, form a family ranging from first-past-the-post to proportional representation as the weight on statewide representation increases. Along this path, gaining further seats through gerrymandering becomes increasingly difficult. The characterization yields a measure of the robustness of first-past-the-post to statewide representation concerns, which we compare with established electoral diagnostics. In U.S. House elections from 2002 to 2024, we find that maps drawn by single-party legislatures perform worse than those produced by courts or non-partisan commissions. The efficiency gap, a common measure of partisan gerrymandering, is more strongly associated with litigated maps than the other measures, yet magnifies the extent to which Republican-legislature maps appear worse than Democratic-legislature maps.
item.dc:creator: Yunus C. Aybas, Oguzhan Celebi, Surabhi Dutt

item.title: Lexicographic Robustness and the Efficiency of Optimal Mechanisms
item.description: arXiv:2604.06105v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The maxmin criterion is commonly used to formalize a mechanism designer's concern for robustness over a set of possible environments. Without substantially restricting this set, however, the criterion may identify a large and economically uninformative collection of mechanisms. This paper proposes a lexicographic, belief-based approach to refining the maxmin criterion and uses it to analyze the efficiency of optimal mechanisms. In canonical screening and auction models, the strongest refinement $\unicode{x2013}$ proper robustness $\unicode{x2013}$ selects ex post efficient mechanisms. By contrast, in a public good provision model, it identifies a unique mechanism whose inefficiency may become severe in large economies.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Kambhampati

item.title: Envy-free, efficient and strategy-proof division of a heterogeneous good between two agents
item.description: arXiv:2606.06059v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the division of $[0,1]$ between two agents, each receiving a closed subinterval, under ordinal preferences that need not be additive. A monotonic preference has a unique balanced cut, at which the agent is indifferent between the left and the right piece. On a domain of monotonic preferences, a strategy-proof, envy-free and Pareto efficient rule exists if and only if the balanced cuts of the preferences in the domain take at most two distinct values; when they take exactly two, the divide-and-choose rules are the only such rules. For preferences single-peaked in quantity, which are additive only if monotonic, the three properties are compatible when the agents' most preferred bundles can be assigned simultaneously.
item.dc:creator: Mihir Bhattacharya, Ojasvi Khare

item.title: Rationalizable Behavior in Matching with Externalities
item.description: arXiv:2606.28028v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In many matching markets, agents care not only about their own partners but also about the matches formed by others. With externalities, stability depends on what agents believe would happen after a deviation. We introduce rationalizable conjectures: beliefs that survive iterated elimination, in the spirit of rationalizability in non-cooperative games. These beliefs define conjecture-rationalizable stability, a solution concept that always exists, extends Gale--Shapley stability, and coincides with it when externalities are absent. We also introduce rationalizable matchings, a non-equilibrium counterpart, and show that every conjecture-rationalizable stable matching is rationalizable. In matching with couples, our concept yields non-empty predictions even when standard stability is vacuous. Finally, we provide an epistemic foundation: rationalizability is behaviorally implied by pairwise rationality and common belief in pairwise rationality, while conjecture-rationalizable stability additionally requires belief correctness.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Nicol\`o, Pietro Salmaso, Riccardo D. Saulle

item.title: The Impossibility of a Gerrymander-Proof Representative Democracy
item.description: arXiv:2607.05660v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A representative democracy is immune to gerrymandering if it satisfies Chambers' (2008) representative consistency. We examine preference aggregation and show that representative consistency is incompatible with three other normative desiderata --- weak Pareto, anonymity, and neutrality. We show this impossibility result both in a setting with ordinal preferences and in a setting with expected utility preferences.
item.dc:creator: John Mori
